propositions.text: Whether self-induced intoxication is a defence to arson under s. 434 of the Criminal Code.
propositions.quote: This case requires the Court to determine whether self-induced intoxication is a defence to a charge of arson under s. 434 of the Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46 .

propositions.text: The charge against Mr. Tatton arose from a fire destroying his ex-girlfriend's home contents.
propositions.quote: The charge against the respondent, Mr. Tatton, arose out of a fire that destroyed the contents of his ex-girlfriend’s home.

propositions.text: Mr. Tatton, intoxicated, placed oil on stove, set burner high, left to get coffee, returned 20 minutes later to find fire.
propositions.quote: The fire began after Mr. Tatton, in a highly intoxicated state, placed a pan with oil on the stove, set the burner to “high”, and left the house to get a coffee at a nearby Tim Hortons. When he returned approximately 20 minutes later, the house was on fire.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the issue is whether self-induced intoxication is a defence to arson; Mr. Tatton caused a fire while intoxicated.

propositions.text: Trial judge found Mr. Tatton could rely on accident defence based on drunkenness to rebut intent for arson.
propositions.quote: At trial, Mr. Tatton sought to rely on the defence of accident based on his drunkenness to rebut the intent required for the offence of arson. The trial judge found that he could do so,

propositions.text: Majority of Court of Appeal agreed with trial judge's finding on intoxication defence.
propositions.quote: and a majority of the Court of Appeal agreed.

propositions.text: Trial judge and majority of Court of Appeal erred; intoxication short of automatism is not a defence to arson under s. 434.
propositions.quote: For reasons that follow, I am respectfully of the view that the trial judge and the majority of the Court of Appeal erred. Intoxication short of automatism is not a defence to a charge of arson under s. 434 of the Criminal Code .

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues intoxication is a defence; earlier decision-makers agreed; the court disagrees and finds intoxication is not a defence.

propositions.text: In September 2010, Mr. Tatton lived in a guest room at ex-girlfriend Ms. Spencer's home after their breakup.
propositions.quote: In September 2010, Mr. Tatton was living in a guest room at a home owned by his ex-girlfriend, Ms. Spencer. He and Ms. Spencer had broken off their relationship, but Mr. Tatton remained hopeful that they would reconcile.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Mr. Tatton lived in his ex-girlfriend's home after their breakup in September 2010.

propositions.text: Mr. Tatton was an alcoholic with binge drinking, blackouts, and past incidents of cooking while drunk and passing out.
propositions.quote: Mr. Tatton was an alcoholic. He had a tendency to binge drink. There was evidence that in the past he had come home drunk, started to cook food, and then passed out, only to awake to a house filled with smoke. His history with alcoholism included periods of blackouts. He would sometimes have no recollection of events that had transpired while he was under the influence of alcohol.

paragraphs.summary: The court describes Mr. Tatton's alcoholism, binge drinking, blackouts, and past incidents involving cooking while drunk.

propositions.text: On Sept 24, 2010, Ms. Spencer left town; Mr. Tatton drank heavily, left agitated messages including references to fire, then passed out.
propositions.quote: On September 24, 2010, Ms. Spencer went to Kingston to visit friends. Mr. Tatton was not happy about this and became jealous and upset. He drank heavily throughout the day and evening, consuming approximately 52 ounces of alcohol. Over the course of the evening, he left Ms. Spencer a series of agitated voice messages on her cell phone, two of which referred to her home being on fire. Eventually, Mr. Tatton passed out.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Mr. Tatton drank heavily and left agitated messages about fire before passing out on Sept 24, 2010.

propositions.text: Mr. Tatton awoke, cooked bacon with oil on stove set to high, left for coffee, returned to find house on fire, called 911, apologized next day.
propositions.quote: When Mr. Tatton awoke, he decided to cook some bacon. He put some vegetable oil in a pan on the stove and set the temperature to “high”. He then drove to a nearby Tim Hortons to get a coffee. When he returned 15-20 minutes later, the house was on fire. Mr. Tatton called 911 from a neighbouring house. The firefighters were able to save the home, but not its contents. The next day, Mr. Tatton left Ms. Spencer a message apologizing for the incident and stating that it was an accident.

paragraphs.summary: The court recounts Mr. Tatton cooking, leaving stove on high, leaving for coffee, returning to fire, calling 911, and apologizing.

propositions.text: Fire investigator found fire source was vegetable oil on stove; Mr. Tatton charged with arson under s. 434 Criminal Code.
propositions.quote: The fire investigator determined that the source of the fire was the vegetable oil on the stove. Mr. Tatton was arrested and charged with arson contrary to s. 434 of the Criminal Code .

propositions.text: Section 434 defines arson as intentional or reckless damage by fire to property not wholly owned by the person, punishable by up to 14 years.
propositions.quote: That section reads: 434. Every person who intentionally or recklessly causes damage by fire or explosion to property that is not wholly owned by that person is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding fourteen years.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the fire source was oil; Mr. Tatton charged with arson under s. 434, which punishes intentional or reckless fire damage.

propositions.text: At trial, Mr. Tatton claimed the fire was an accident, thought stove was on low, lacked intent or foresight of damage.
propositions.quote: At trial, Mr. Tatton claimed that the fire was an accident. When he put the oil on the stove, he thought he had set the temperature at “low”. He did not intend or foresee the consequences that resulted from his turning the stove on and leaving it unattended.

propositions.text: Central trial question was whether Mr. Tatton had requisite intent for arson and whether intoxication could be considered.
propositions.quote: A central question at trial was whether Mr. Tatton had the requisite intent to commit the offence of arson under s. 434 , and more particularly whether the court could take his state of intoxication into account in making its assessment.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker reports Mr. Tatton claimed accident and lack of intent; trial focused on intent and intoxication relevance.

propositions.text: Trial judge found s. 434 a specific intent offence, allowing intoxication defence, and acquitted Mr. Tatton for lack of proof of intent.
propositions.quote: The trial judge determined that s. 434 was a specific intent offence, meaning that Mr. Tatton could rely on self-induced intoxication as a defence. In the end, he acquitted Mr. Tatton because he was not convinced beyond a reasonable doubt that Mr. Tatton intentionally or recklessly left the stove on “high”.

propositions.text: Trial judge not satisfied Mr. Tatton intentionally or recklessly damaged property, acquitted him.
propositions.quote: Given this conclusion, he could not be satisfied that Mr. Tatton intentionally or recklessly damaged the property. A majority of the Court of Appeal for Ontario upheld Mr. Tatton’s acquittal.

propositions.text: Majority of Court of Appeal upheld acquittal; one dissenting member would have ordered new trial.
propositions.quote: A majority of the Court of Appeal for Ontario upheld Mr. Tatton’s acquittal. The third member of the panel would have allowed the appeal and ordered a new trial.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker found s. 434 specific intent, acquitted Mr. Tatton; majority Court of Appeal upheld acquittal; dissent wanted new trial.

propositions.text: Crown appeals arguing arson under s. 434 is general intent offence; intoxication short of automatism not a defence.
propositions.quote: The Crown appeals to this Court as of right. It argues that arson contrary to s. 434 is a general intent offence, meaning that intoxication falling short of automatism cannot be considered.

propositions.text: Court agrees arson under s. 434 is general intent offence; intoxication short of automatism not a defence; orders new trial.
propositions.quote: I agree. I further agree that a new trial is required because the trial judge’s critical findings of fact were tainted by his belief that self-induced intoxication was relevant to the issue of intent. Accordingly, I would allow the appeal, set aside the verdict of acquittal, and order a new trial.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant Crown argues arson is general intent; the court agrees and orders a new trial due to trial judge's error.

propositions.text: Live issue at trial was whether Mr. Tatton caused fire intentionally or recklessly to infer intent for arson.
propositions.quote: The only live issue before the trial judge was whether Mr. Tatton had caused the fire intentionally or recklessly. If so, it could be inferred, in the circumstances, that in setting the fire he either intended to cause damage to the contents of the home or was reckless whether damage ensued or not.

propositions.text: If fire caused by accident or negligence, intent for arson could not be inferred.
propositions.quote: On the other hand, if the fire started by reason of accident or negligence, then it could not be inferred that Mr. Tatton had one of the intents required to support a conviction under s. 434 .

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker states the trial issue was whether fire was intentional or reckless, affecting inference of intent for arson.

propositions.text: Trial judge found Mr. Tatton heavily intoxicated at fire time; needed to determine if s. 434 was specific or general intent offence.
propositions.quote: The trial judge found that Mr. Tatton was heavily under the influence of alcohol at the time of the fire. Consequently, he held that it was necessary to determine whether arson was a crime of specific or general intent.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker found Mr. Tatton intoxicated and that classification of s. 434 as specific or general intent was necessary.

propositions.text: Trial judge concluded s. 434 classification depends on facts, especially how fire started.
propositions.quote: The trial judge concluded that the characterization of s. 434 as either an offence of general or specific intent was fact-driven. In his view, the proper characterization depended on how the fire started.

propositions.text: If fire started with match and combustibles, arson likely general intent; nuanced start could be specific intent.
propositions.quote: If an accused started a fire with a match and combustible material, the charge of arson would likely be one of general intent. However, if the way in which the fire started was more nuanced, it could be a specific intent offence.

propositions.text: On facts, trial judge found s. 434 specific intent; acquitted Mr. Tatton for lack of proof of intentional or reckless stove setting.
propositions.quote: On the facts before him, the trial judge found that the offence was one of specific intent, such that Mr. Tatton’s state of intoxication could be considered. In the end, he was not “satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that [Mr. Tatton] left the setting [on the stove] on ‘high’ either intentionally or recklessly”: A.R., vol. I, at p. 81. Accordingly, he acquitted Mr. Tatton on the charge of arson.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker found s. 434 classification fact-driven, found it specific intent here, and acquitted Mr. Tatton.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal unanimously rejected trial judge's fact-driven classification of s. 434; held classification is a question of law.
propositions.quote: The Court of Appeal unanimously rejected the trial judge’s conclusion that the characterization of s. 434 as an offence of general or specific intent was fact-driven and dependent on how the fire started. Rather, the court determined — correctly in my view — that the characterization of s. 434 amounted to a question of law.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal divided on classification question.
propositions.quote: On that question, the court divided.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker reports Court of Appeal held s. 434 classification is a legal question and was divided on it.

propositions.text: Majority of Court of Appeal characterized arson under s. 434 as specific intent offence requiring voluntary act and awareness of consequences.
propositions.quote: Writing for the majority, Pardu J.A. characterized arson under s. 434 as a specific intent offence. In her view, s. 434 required a voluntary act, coupled with an awareness of the more distant consequences of that act, and a decision to proceed in the face of those consequences.

propositions.text: Majority noted many household activities cause fires but do not imply intentional or reckless damage; no basis intoxication caused household fires.
propositions.quote: Justice Pardu noted that many ordinary household activities cause fires; however, they do not lead inevitably to the conclusion that the person intentionally or recklessly damaged property. Furthermore, there was no basis to conclude that intoxication played a significant role in causing household fires.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker reports majority Court of Appeal found s. 434 specific intent, requiring awareness and decision despite consequences.

propositions.text: Majority held if s. 434 were general intent, mens rea would be objective, not subjective; 'intentionally or recklessly' requires subjective mens rea.
propositions.quote: Justice Pardu also maintained that if arson were to be characterized as a general intent offence, the mens rea for the offence would be objective, not subjective. In her view, the words “intentionally or recklessly” require consideration of an accused’s subjective state of mind, to which intoxication is relevant.

propositions.text: Majority upheld Mr. Tatton’s acquittal as s. 434 is specific intent offence.
propositions.quote: Consequently, she found that s. 434 was a specific intent offence, and upheld Mr. Tatton’s acquittal.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker reports majority held s. 434 specific intent, requiring subjective mens rea, and upheld acquittal.

propositions.text: Dissenting judge held s. 434 is general intent offence; intoxication short of automatism not a defence.
propositions.quote: In dissent, Goudge J.A. concluded that s. 434 was a general intent offence and that intoxication short of automatism could therefore not be considered.

propositions.text: Dissent held mens rea did not extend beyond actus reus; no ulterior purpose required.
propositions.quote: He held that the mens rea for s. 434 did not extend beyond the actus reus, and that no ulterior purpose was required.

propositions.text: Dissent noted arson is often committed when intoxicated; policy reasons to refuse intoxication defence.
propositions.quote: He was also of the view that arson is the type of offence that people are apt to commit when intoxicated; therefore, there were good policy reasons for refusing to allow an accused to raise the defence of self-induced intoxication.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker reports dissent held s. 434 general intent, no intoxication defence, and cited policy reasons.

propositions.text: Dissent disagreed that excluding intoxication made mens rea objective; inquiry remains subjective to accused's sober foresight.
propositions.quote: Justice Goudge disagreed with the majority that precluding reliance on intoxication transformed the mens rea inquiry into an objective one. In his view, the inquiry does not ask if a reasonable person would have foreseen the risk of damage to property; rather, one asks if the particular accused, while sober, would have foreseen the risk.

propositions.text: Dissent concluded s. 434 not specific intent offence; trial judge erred; error materially affected outcome; new trial warranted.
propositions.quote: This approach retained the necessary subjective component of the mens rea. It followed that arson under s. 434 was not a specific intent offence and that the trial judge erred in concluding otherwise. Justice Goudge held that the error had a material bearing on the outcome. Hence, he would have ordered a new trial.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker reports dissent held mens rea inquiry remains subjective, s. 434 not specific intent, trial judge erred, new trial needed.

propositions.text: Two issues on appeal: classification of arson under s. 434 as general or specific intent; and if general intent, whether trial judge's error materially affected verdict.
propositions.quote: There are two issues on appeal: 1. Is arson contrary to s. 434 a general or specific intent offence? 2. If arson contrary to s. 434 is a general intent offence, did the trial judge’s error have a material bearing on the verdict?

paragraphs.summary: The court states the two issues on appeal: classification of arson offence and materiality of trial judge's error if general intent.

propositions.text: Classification as general or specific intent affects intoxication defence availability; intoxication short of automatism not defence for general intent offences.
propositions.quote: The classification of an offence as one involving general or specific intent has important consequences for the accused. The law does not allow offenders to rely on self-induced intoxication falling short of automatism as an excuse for general intent offences: R. v. Daviault, [1994] 3 S.C.R. 63, at p. 123; R. v. Bernard, [1988] 2 S.C.R. 833, at pp. 865 and 878-80.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains classification affects intoxication defence; intoxication short of automatism not defence for general intent offences.

propositions.text: Labels 'general intent' and 'specific intent' are entrenched but not helpful to describe the mental element of a crime.
propositions.quote: Although the labels “general intent” and “specific intent” are entrenched in Canadian law, they are not particularly helpful in describing the actual mental element required for a crime

propositions.text: The distinction lies in complexity of thought and social policy underlying the offence.
propositions.quote: the distinction lies in the complexity of the thought and reasoning processes that make up the mental element of a particular offence, and the social policy underlying the offence

paragraphs.summary: The court finds that 'general intent' and 'specific intent' labels are entrenched but unhelpful; distinction lies in mental complexity and social policy.

propositions.text: Daviault is leading case on general/specific intent but confusion remains.
propositions.quote: This Court’s decision in Daviault is the leading case on the distinction between general and specific intent crimes. Unfortunately, it has not resolved the confusion surrounding this issue.

propositions.text: General/specific intent dichotomy criticized as illogical and inconsistent across courts and jurisdictions.
propositions.quote: It has been criticized as illogical and as leading to “arbitrary and inconsistent results from court to court, offence to offence and jurisdiction to jurisdiction”

propositions.text: Several academic sources criticize the general/specific intent distinction.
propositions.quote: See also T. Quigley, “Specific and General Nonsense?” (1987), 11 Dal. L.J. 75; D. Stuart, Canadian Criminal Law: A Treatise (5th ed. 2007), at pp. 437-39; M. Manning, Q.C., and P. Sankoff, Manning, Mewett & Sankoff: Criminal Law (4th ed. 2009), at p. 389; S. H. Berner, “The Defense of Drunkenness — A Reconsideration” (1971), 6 U.B.C. L. Rev. 309, at pp. 333-34.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Daviault is leading but confusing; prior authorities criticize the general/specific intent distinction as illogical and inconsistent.

propositions.text: Criminal Code often lacks clear direction on mental element, leaving judges to divine fault requirement.
propositions.quote: the Criminal Code often provides no clear direction about the required mental element for a given offence. It is therefore left to judges to attempt to divine the required mental element

propositions.text: Professor Don Stuart states confusion on fault requirement undermines legitimacy of adversary system and presumption of innocence.
propositions.quote: Our adversary system, which requires cases to be fairly put to impartial judges or juries, and the presumption of innocence, cannot work with legitimacy where there is confusion as to the applicable tests on even basic matters such as the fault requirement

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Criminal Code lacks clear mental element guidance; Stuart says this confusion undermines legitimacy of justice system.

propositions.text: Academics and law reform bodies urge Criminal Code amendments to specify mental element and fault for each crime.
propositions.quote: He and other academics and law reform bodies have urged that the Criminal Code be amended to specify the mental element and fault requirement for each crime

propositions.text: Several reports and proposals have recommended clarifying mental elements in Criminal Code.
propositions.quote: see, e.g., Law Reform Commission of Canada, Report on Recodifying Criminal Law (1987), at pp. 17 and 21-25; Canadian Bar Association’s Criminal Recodification Task Force, Principles of Criminal Liability: Proposals for a New General Part of the Criminal Code of Canada (1992), at pp. 41-49; D. Stuart, “A Case for a General Part”

paragraphs.summary: The court reports academics and reform bodies urge Criminal Code amendments to clarify mental elements, citing several reports.

propositions.text: Difficulty in classifying offences as general or specific intent stems from lack of legislative clarity on mental elements and intoxication defence.
propositions.quote: The shortcoming identified by Professor Stuart and other scholars is the source of the difficulty in determining whether an offence is one of general or specific intent

propositions.text: Legislative intervention needed to clarify mental elements and intoxication defence; meanwhile existing regime applies.
propositions.quote: Legislative intervention is sorely needed to spell out the mental element of offences and to specify when intoxication short of automatism can be considered. However, until that day comes we are left with the existing regime

propositions.text: Before classifying s. 434 offence, court will review Daviault analysis to clarify general/specific intent distinction.
propositions.quote: before turning to the proper classification of the offence in s. 434 of the Criminal Code , I propose to review the analysis in Daviault in the hope of shedding a bit more light on the general/specific intent distinction

paragraphs.summary: The court finds legislative clarity needed on mental elements; until then, it reviews Daviault to clarify general/specific intent for s. 434 offence.

propositions.text: Daviault examined intoxication defence for general intent crimes and discussed general/specific intent distinction at length.
propositions.quote: In Daviault, this Court examined whether an accused who is in a state of extreme intoxication, akin to automatism, may rely on drunkenness as a defence to a general intent crime. In analysing this issue, the distinction between general and specific intent offences was discussed at some length by Sopinka J.

propositions.text: Sopinka J. held two factors distinguish general from specific intent crimes: nature/importance of mental element and social policy.
propositions.quote: He held that two factors help distinguish crimes of general intent from those of specific intent: first, “[t]he nature of the mental element and its relative importance” and second, “the social policy sought to be attained by criminalizing the particular conduct”

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision in Daviault found two factors distinguish general and specific intent: mental element's nature and social policy.

propositions.text: General intent crimes involve minimal intent to do the act constituting actus reus.
propositions.quote: Justice Sopinka specified that general intent crimes involve “the minimal intent to do the act which constitutes the actus reus”

propositions.text: High intoxication short of automatism unlikely to negate minimal mental acuity for general intent crimes.
propositions.quote: even a high degree of intoxication short of automatism is unlikely to deprive the accused of the slight degree of mental acuity required to commit them

propositions.text: Allowing intoxication defence for general intent crimes contradicts social policy as drunk persons apt to commit such offences.
propositions.quote: general intent crimes tend to be “offences that persons who are drunk are apt to commit”... allowing intoxication to operate as a defence would contradict the social policy underlying these crimes

propositions.text: Intent can be inferred from act performance for minimal mental element crimes.
propositions.quote: one can typically infer intent from the performance of the act

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision found general intent crimes require minimal intent, intoxication defence unlikely, and policy opposes intoxication defence.

propositions.text: Specific intent crimes require heightened mental element involving ulterior motives or purposes.
propositions.quote: specific intent crimes require a heightened mental element. For example, they often require “the formation of further ulterior motives and purposes”

propositions.text: Intoxication short of automatism may negate mental element for specific intent crimes.
propositions.quote: one can readily understand how intoxication short of automatism may negate the required mental element

propositions.text: Specific intent offences less likely to be committed by intoxicated persons; policy concerns less pressing.
propositions.quote: specific intent offences are less likely to be the type of offences that intoxicated people are apt to commit. For that reason, policy considerations that might otherwise militate against a defence of intoxication are less pressing

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision found specific intent crimes require heightened mental element; intoxication may negate it; policy concerns less pressing.

propositions.text: Specific intent offences often include lesser general intent offences, so intoxicated offenders may still be punished.
propositions.quote: specific intent offences often include lesser offences that only require general intent. In such cases, an intoxicated offender will not escape punishment altogether

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision found specific intent offences include lesser general intent offences, so intoxicated offenders may still be punished.

propositions.text: Classification of offence as general or specific intent starts with determining the mental element by statutory interpretation.
propositions.quote: The analysis of whether an offence is one of specific or general intent must start with a determination of the mental element of the offence in question. This is an exercise in statutory interpretation

propositions.text: Mental element determination should not be a factual assessment based on case circumstances.
propositions.quote: Care should be taken not to turn it into a factual assessment based on the circumstances of the particular case

paragraphs.summary: The court rules classification starts with statutory interpretation of mental element, not factual assessment of case circumstances.

propositions.text: Next question is whether crime is general or specific intent; distinction involves logic, intuition, and policy.
propositions.quote: After the mental element of the provision has been determined, the next question is whether the crime is one of general or specific intent. The distinction between general and specific intent offences is not a precise science. Logic, intuition, and policy all play a part

propositions.text: Distinction is formidable for criminal law experts and daunting for others.
propositions.quote: The task has proved formidable to those who have been schooled in criminal law, and daunting to those who have not

paragraphs.summary: The court finds classifying crime as general or specific intent involves logic, intuition, policy, and is difficult even for experts.

propositions.text: Start classification by looking to existing jurisprudence; if clear, no need to re-examine.
propositions.quote: the place to begin in determining the appropriate classification of the offence is to look to existing jurisprudence. Where the jurisprudence has already determined the appropriate classification of the offence in a satisfactory manner, the task is straightforward

propositions.text: Sexual assault is general intent; robbery and murder are specific intent offences per prior cases.
propositions.quote: this Court has established that sexual assault is a general intent offence, whereas robbery and murder are specific intent offences

propositions.text: Framework clarifies but does not change Daviault law; unclear jurisprudence requires examining Daviault factors.
propositions.quote: The framework that follows is meant to clarify, not change the law as set out in Daviault. However, if the jurisprudence is unclear, courts must examine the factors outlined in Daviault, as clarified below, to resolve the question

paragraphs.summary: The court rules classification starts with existing jurisprudence; if unclear, examine Daviault factors; framework clarifies but does not change law.

propositions.text: Daviault left unclear what 'importance' of mental element means and when policy considerations apply.
propositions.quote: it left certain questions unanswered. First, it provided no clear explanation of what is meant by the “importance” of the mental element. Second, it did not specify whether policy considerations should always play a role in the analysis or whether they should only come into play if an examination of the mental element left unclear how the offence should be characterized

propositions.text: Court will address these questions to clarify the law.
propositions.quote: I turn to these questions in the hope of bringing some added clarity to an area of the law that continues to perplex and confound

paragraphs.summary: The court identifies issues left by Daviault on 'importance' of mental element and role of policy, and will clarify them.

propositions.text: Daviault's 'importance' of mental element means complexity of thought and reasoning processes.
propositions.quote: it is clear that he was referring to the complexity of the thought and reasoning processes that make up the mental element of a particular offence

paragraphs.summary: The court finds 'importance' of mental element means complexity of thought and reasoning processes.

propositions.text: General intent crimes mental element relates to performing illegal act, no intent to cause external consequences required.
propositions.quote: For general intent crimes, the mental element simply relates to the performance of an illegal act. Such crimes do not require an intent to bring about certain consequences that are external to the actus reus

propositions.text: Assault is classic general intent crime requiring intentional force but not intent to cause injury.
propositions.quote: Assault is a classic example. The accused must intentionally apply force; however, there is no requirement that he intend to cause injury

propositions.text: General intent crimes do not require actual knowledge of circumstances if knowledge requires complex reasoning.
propositions.quote: crimes of general intent do not require actual knowledge of certain circumstances or consequences, to the extent that such knowledge is the product of complex thought and reasoning processes

propositions.text: Mental element for general intent crimes is straightforward and requires little mental acuity.
propositions.quote: In each instance, the mental element is straightforward and requires little mental acuity

paragraphs.summary: The court finds general intent crimes require intent to do act, not intent to cause consequences or complex knowledge; mental element is straightforward.

propositions.text: 'Straightforward' mental element means same as Daviault's 'minimal intent' and 'minimal degree of consciousness'.
propositions.quote: I am using these phrases synonymously with the descriptors used in Daviault: “minimal intent” and “minimal degree of consciousness”

paragraphs.summary: The court clarifies 'straightforward' mental element means same as Daviault's 'minimal intent' and 'minimal degree of consciousness'.

propositions.text: Specific intent offences require ulterior purpose beyond actus reus, e.g. assault with intent to resist arrest.
propositions.quote: For such crimes, the accused must not only intend to do the act that constitutes the actus reus, he must also act with an ulterior purpose in mind

paragraphs.summary: The court finds specific intent offences require ulterior purpose beyond actus reus, e.g. assault with intent to resist arrest.

propositions.text: Heightened mental element may be ulterior purpose, intent to cause consequences, or actual knowledge requiring complex reasoning.
propositions.quote: a heightened mental element could take the form of a requirement that the accused intend and bring about certain consequences, if the formation of that intent involves more complex thought and reasoning processes

propositions.text: Murder is example of intent to cause consequences; possession of stolen property requires actual knowledge, both specific intent.
propositions.quote: Murder provides a classic example... Possession of stolen property is one such crime. The accused must actually know or be willfully blind to the fact that the goods he or she possesses are stolen

propositions.text: Intoxication defence available for specific intent crimes with complex mental elements.
propositions.quote: Intoxication is therefore available as a defence for such crimes

paragraphs.summary: The court finds heightened mental element includes ulterior purpose, intent to cause consequences, or actual knowledge; intoxication defence applies.

propositions.text: Specific intent offences have heightened mental element; general intent offences require little mental acuity.
propositions.quote: specific intent offences contain a heightened mental element... General intent offences, on the other hand, require very little mental acuity

paragraphs.summary: The court summarizes specific intent offences have heightened mental element; general intent offences require little mental acuity.

propositions.text: Daviault left unclear when policy considerations should be considered in classification analysis.
propositions.quote: The second question that Daviault left unanswered is the stage at which policy ought to be considered

propositions.text: Unclear if policy applies always or only if mental element analysis is unclear.
propositions.quote: Confusion remains about whether policy should be considered in every case or whether it should only come into play if an examination of the mental element leaves it unclear how the offence should be characterized

paragraphs.summary: The court identifies issue left by Daviault on when policy considerations apply in classification analysis.

propositions.text: Examine the nature of the mental element first before considering policy in intoxication defence cases.
propositions.quote: the most logical approach is to first examine the nature of the mental element. Only when this analysis fails to yield a clear answer should one turn to policy considerations.

propositions.text: Daviault explains general intent crimes involve minimal mental acuity, making intoxication defence unavailable for them.
propositions.quote: General intent crimes involve such minimal mental acuity that it is difficult to see how intoxication short of automatism could deprive the accused of the low level of intent required. This provides a strong policy reason for precluding reliance on intoxication for these offences: Daviault, at p. 123.

propositions.text: It is constitutionally permissible to deny intoxication defence for general intent offences.
propositions.quote: It also explains why it is constitutionally permissible to render the intoxication defence unavailable for general intent offences: ibid., at pp. 99-100.

propositions.text: Specific intent crimes require complex thought, so intoxication may negate intent and be considered as defence.
propositions.quote: one can more readily understand how the more complex thought and reasoning processes required for specific intent crimes may be negated by an accused’s intoxication. For that reason, policy suggests that intoxication can be considered for specific intent crimes.

propositions.text: If mental element analysis clearly characterizes the offence, policy considerations are unnecessary.
propositions.quote: if an examination of the mental element clearly indicates how the offence should be characterized, there is little reason to resort to policy considerations.

paragraphs.summary: The court states mental element should be examined first to classify offences for intoxication defence, citing Daviault on general and specific intent distinctions.

propositions.text: If mental element analysis is unclear, policy considerations help decide intoxication defence availability.
propositions.quote: if an examination of the mental element does not provide a clear answer, policy considerations may help resolve the question.

propositions.text: Policy focuses on whether alcohol consumption is habitually associated with the crime.
propositions.quote: the policy assessment will focus on whether alcohol consumption is habitually associated with the crime in question.

propositions.text: Intoxication is often associated with sexual assault, so allowing intoxication defence would endorse problematic behaviour.
propositions.quote: intoxication is often associated with the crime of sexual assault. Allowing self-induced intoxication to provide an accused with a defence would be to endorse, if not promote, the very behaviour that has historically proved to be a root cause of the problem.

propositions.text: Where intoxication rarely plays a role in a crime, denying intoxication defence makes less policy sense.
propositions.quote: where self-induced intoxication rarely, if ever, plays a role in the commission of a particular crime, preventing an accused from relying on it makes less sense from a policy perspective.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains policy considerations focus on habitual alcohol association with crimes, affecting intoxication defence availability.

propositions.text: Alcohol often plays a role in violent or unruly conduct and property damage crimes, so intoxication defence is generally inappropriate.
propositions.quote: alcohol habitually plays a role in crimes involving violent or unruly conduct: Bernard, at p. 880. It also tends to be prevalent in crimes involving damage to property. As such, it makes little sense from a policy perspective that it should provide a defence for crimes in which people or property are harmed or endangered: Daviault, at p. 123.

propositions.text: Murder is a specific intent crime allowing intoxication defence due to complex reasoning, gravity, punishment, and lesser included offence.
propositions.quote: Murder, for example, has long been considered a crime of specific intent for which the defence of intoxication is available. As Daviault explains, at p. 124, this is a function of the heightened thought and reasoning processes required, the gravity of the offence, the serious fixed punishment upon conviction, and the availability of the lesser included offence of manslaughter.

propositions.text: Intoxication may be considered in violent or property damage crimes, but strong policy reasons usually oppose it.
propositions.quote: it is therefore incorrect to state that intoxication may never be considered in crimes involving violence against people or damage to property. However, given the prevalence of alcohol in these crimes, there are likely to be strong policy reasons militating against an intoxication-based defence.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes alcohol's role in violent and property crimes, allowing intoxication defence in murder but generally opposing it for others.

propositions.text: Presence of lesser included general intent offence may allow intoxication defence for main offence without escaping punishment.
propositions.quote: the presence of a lesser included general intent offence in the main offence may be relevant. In such cases, an accused who successfully relies on intoxication to negate the heightened mental element of the main offence can still be convicted of the lesser included offence. Drunkenness will provide no defence to the lesser offence.

propositions.text: Example: intoxication defence to assault with intent to resist arrest may still lead to conviction for assault.
propositions.quote: For example, an accused who successfully raises intoxication as a defence to a charge of assault with intent to resist arrest may still be convicted of the lesser included offence of assault.

propositions.text: Intoxicated offenders won't escape punishment if lesser offence conviction remains, reducing need to preclude intoxication defence.
propositions.quote: In these situations, the intoxicated offender will not escape punishment altogether. Consequently, there is less impetus to preclude the accused from advancing intoxication as a defence to the main offence.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains lesser included offences may allow intoxication defence without total punishment escape, reducing reasons to preclude defence.

propositions.text: Judicial sentencing discretion may affect whether intoxication defence should be allowed.
propositions.quote: the presence of judicial sentencing discretion may be a factor to consider.

propositions.text: Heavy minimum sentences may make precluding intoxication defence harsh; sentencing discretion lessens this concern.
propositions.quote: If the crime is one for which the accused will receive a heavy minimum sentence upon conviction, it may be unduly harsh to preclude consideration of intoxication. However, if the judge has discretion to tailor the sentence to the facts of the case and to consider the accused’s intoxication as part of that assessment, precluding the accused from advancing a defence of intoxication is less worrisome: Daviault, at p. 124.

paragraphs.summary: The court states sentencing discretion affects the appropriateness of precluding intoxication defence, citing Daviault.

propositions.text: Arson offence in s. 434 has a long history with courts divided on general or specific intent classification.
propositions.quote: The crime of arson has existed for many years, and the Criminal Code provisions have gone through many iterations. Over the years, courts have been divided on whether the offence of arson in s. 434 (and its predecessors) is a crime of general or specific intent: see, e.g., R. v. Swanson (1989), 48 C.C.C. (3d) 316 (Y.T.C.A.) (specific intent); R. v. Hudson (1993), 88 Man. R. (2d) 150 (C.A.) (specific intent); and R. v. Muma (1989), 51 C.C.C. (3d) 85 (Ont. C.A.) (general intent), relying on R. v. Schmidtke (1985), 19 C.C.C. (3d) 390 (Ont. C.A.).

paragraphs.summary: The court notes historical division among courts on whether s. 434 arson is general or specific intent offence.

propositions.text: Section 434 arson is a general intent offence; intoxication short of automatism is not a defence.
propositions.quote: I am satisfied that s. 434 is a general intent offence for which intoxication falling short of automatism is not available as a defence.

propositions.text: Section 434 provision states intentional or reckless damage by fire to property not wholly owned by accused is indictable offence.
propositions.quote: 434. Every person who intentionally or recklessly causes damage by fire or explosion to property that is not wholly owned by that person is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding fourteen years.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes s. 434 arson is general intent offence without intoxication defence, quoting the provision.

propositions.text: Actus reus is damaging property by fire; mental element is intentional or reckless causing of damage; no complex reasoning needed.
propositions.quote: The actus reus is the damaging of property by fire. The mental element is the intentional or reckless performance of the illegal act — the causing of damage to property. No additional knowledge or purpose is needed. No complex thought or reasoning processes are required.

propositions.text: The level of intent required for s. 434 appears minimal.
propositions.quote: On its face, the level of intent required for the offence would appear to be minimal.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds s. 434 requires minimal intent: intentional or reckless damage by fire without complex reasoning.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal majority worried that classifying s. 434 as general intent would make recklessness an objective inquiry.
propositions.quote: A majority of the Court of Appeal was concerned that if s. 434 were found to be a general intent offence, so as to preclude consideration of intoxication short of automatism, that would improperly transform the examination of recklessness into an objective inquiry.

propositions.text: The court disagrees; recklessness is subjective and involves seeing risk and acting regardless.
propositions.quote: With respect, I cannot agree. Recklessness describes the act of one who sees the risk and acts without regard for the consequences: Sansregret v. The Queen, [1985] 1 S.C.R. 570, at p. 582. It always involves a subjective inquiry — and this case is no exception.

propositions.text: S. 434 arson does not involve sophisticated reasoning; risk of damage by fire is typically obvious.
propositions.quote: However, the offence of arson under s. 434 does not involve sophisticated reasoning. The risk of damage by fire is typically obvious, even when it involves a chain of events and not the simple application of a match to the property in question.

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects Court of Appeal's concern, affirming recklessness is subjective and s. 434 involves obvious risk without complex reasoning.

propositions.text: Intoxication short of automatism unlikely to prevent accused from foreseeing risk of property damage by fire.
propositions.quote: I have difficulty seeing how intoxication short of automatism would prevent an accused from foreseeing the risk of causing damage to someone else’s property by fire.

propositions.text: Preventing intoxication defence does not make recklessness objective but recognizes minimal intent remains despite intoxication.
propositions.quote: Thus, preventing an accused from advancing the defence of intoxication does not transform recklessness into an objective inquiry. Rather, it recognizes the fact that intoxication short of automatism will not deprive an accused of the minimal intent required for this crime.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds intoxication short of automatism won't negate minimal intent, so denying intoxication defence doesn't make recklessness objective.

propositions.text: No need to use policy considerations to decide intoxication defence availability for s. 434 given mental element analysis.
propositions.quote: In view of this conclusion, there is no need to resort to policy considerations to determine the availability of the defence of intoxication.

propositions.text: If policy considerations were needed, court would still conclude intoxication defence unavailable for s. 434.
propositions.quote: However, had I found it necessary to do so, I would have reached the same conclusion.

paragraphs.summary: The court says mental element analysis suffices to deny intoxication defence for s. 434, but policy would also support that conclusion.

propositions.text: Section 434 involves property damage often associated with alcohol; intoxication defence would undermine offence policy.
propositions.quote: Section 434 involves damage to property. Damage to property is often associated with alcohol consumption. The present case is no exception. In my view, it would erode the policy underlying the offence of causing damage to property by fire if an accused could rely on self-induced intoxication as a defence.

paragraphs.summary: The court states property damage in s. 434 is often linked to alcohol, so intoxication defence would undermine policy.

propositions.text: Trial judge and Court of Appeal erred in classifying s. 434 as specific intent allowing intoxication defence.
propositions.quote: For these reasons, I am respectfully of the view that the trial judge and the majority of the Court of Appeal erred in characterizing s. 434 as a specific intent offence for which the defence of intoxication could be raised.

propositions.text: Proper classification of s. 434 is general intent, so intoxication short of automatism is not considered.
propositions.quote: Properly classified, s. 434 is a general intent offence, meaning that intoxication short of automatism may not be considered.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes s. 434 is general intent offence, so intoxication defence is unavailable, reversing trial judge and Court of Appeal.

propositions.text: Determining intent under s. 434 can be complex due to varied factual scenarios.
propositions.quote: Leaving aside the question of intoxication, ascertaining whether the intent required under s. 434 has been made out in a particular case can be a tricky exercise.

propositions.text: Trial judge and Court of Appeal noted wide range of factual scenarios under s. 434.
propositions.quote: As the trial judge and the majority of the Court of Appeal noted, there is a wide range of factual scenarios that may arise under s. 434 of the Criminal Code.

propositions.text: Some cases involve direct fire setting; others involve causing an object to catch fire leading to property damage.
propositions.quote: Some cases may involve an accused who has set fire directly to the property in issue. Others, like this one, may involve an accused who has caused some object to catch fire, which in turn leads to damage to property.

propositions.text: Direct fire setting cases usually allow inference of intentional or reckless damage; indirect cases may not.
propositions.quote: In the former, there is typically a ready-made inference that the accused intentionally or recklessly caused damage by fire. In the latter, such an inference may not be so obvious, and the assessment of intent can be obtuse.

propositions.text: Court offers suggestions to help triers of fact decide if requisite intent is established under s. 434.
propositions.quote: Without setting out a legal framework, I offer some suggestions that triers of fact may find helpful in deciding whether the requisite intent has been established.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes intent under s. 434 can be complex and offers guidance for fact-finders on varied scenarios.

propositions.text: The criminal act in s. 434 is causing damage to property, not setting fire itself; fire is the damage mechanism.
propositions.quote: To begin, it must be remembered that the criminal act in s. 434 is not the setting of a fire. The conduct that has been criminalized is the causing of damage to property. The fire is simply the mechanism by which the damage must be caused. This distinction is crucial to the analysis.

paragraphs.summary: The court clarifies s. 434 criminalizes causing property damage, not just setting fire, which is the damage mechanism.

propositions.text: Trier of fact must consider all circumstances, including how fire started, in intent assessment under s. 434.
propositions.quote: In assessing the issue of intent, the trier of fact must of course consider all of the surrounding circumstances. How the fire started is likely to be an important consideration.

propositions.text: Whether fire was accidental, negligent, reckless, or intentional is important but not dispositive for intent under s. 434.
propositions.quote: Specifically, was the fire set accidentally, negligently, recklessly, or intentionally? The answer to this question will not be dispositive since, as I have explained, the act of setting a fire is not the conduct that has been criminalized under s. 434 . Nonetheless, it will provide important context for the intent analysis.

paragraphs.summary: The court instructs fact-finders to consider all circumstances, including fire origin, as context for intent under s. 434.

propositions.text: Intent analysis focuses on whether accused intentionally or recklessly caused property damage, not just on how fire started.
propositions.quote: the end game involves looking at all of the surrounding circumstances to determine whether it can be inferred that the accused intended to cause damage to someone else’s property or was reckless whether damage ensued or not.

propositions.text: Intent to set fire may not equal intent or recklessness to cause property damage; context is key.
propositions.quote: The mere fact that the fire was set intentionally or recklessly may not be enough to establish that the accused intentionally or recklessly caused damage to the property. Context is important and will play a key role in determining whether such an inference can be drawn.

propositions.text: Example: controlled fire in fire pit causing accidental damage to neighbour's shed may not show intent or recklessness to damage shed.
propositions.quote: Consider, for instance, a homeowner who has started a controlled fire in an outdoor fire pit. If a gust of wind picks up some burning leaves from the fire pit and blows them onto a neighbour’s shed 20 metres away, it does not follow that he intentionally or recklessly damaged the shed: see, e.g., R. v. S.D.D., 2002 NFCA 18, 211 Nfld. & P.E.I.R. 157.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains intent to cause damage under s. 434 depends on context, not just intentional fire setting, citing example case.

propositions.text: If accused deliberately sets fire and does nothing to stop damage, intent or recklessness to cause damage may be inferred.
propositions.quote: In contrast, there are many situations in which an accused has intentionally or recklessly started a fire and the surrounding circumstances make it clear that he or she intended to cause damage to property or was reckless whether damage ensued.

propositions.text: Example: setting fire to towel and leaving it to burn carpet may infer intent or recklessness to cause damage.
propositions.quote: Take, for instance, a person who has deliberately set fire to a towel. If that person were to drop the towel on the carpet and walk away without making any effort to extinguish the fire, it may be inferred that he or she intended to cause damage to property or was reckless whether damage ensued.

paragraphs.summary: The court states deliberate fire setting with no effort to stop damage may infer intent or recklessness to cause property damage.

propositions.text: Guilt under s. 434 depends on intentional or reckless causing of property damage, not on how fire started.
propositions.quote: An accused’s guilt under s. 434 hinges on whether he or she intentionally or recklessly caused damage to the property in question.

propositions.text: Triers of fact must keep distinction between setting fire and causing damage in mind and examine context for intent analysis.
propositions.quote: So long as the trier of fact keeps this important distinction in mind and examines the relevant context and surrounding circumstances, the analysis of intent under s. 434 should be relatively straightforward.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes s. 434 guilt depends on intent or recklessness to cause damage, requiring context and distinction from fire setting.

propositions.text: Crown must show trial judge's error might have materially affected acquittal to obtain new trial.
propositions.quote: To obtain a new trial, the Crown must demonstrate that the error might reasonably have had a material bearing on the acquittal.

propositions.text: R. v. Graveline requires Crown to show error had material bearing on acquittal, not just hypothetical possibility.
propositions.quote: As this Court explained in R. v. Graveline, 2006 SCC 16, [2006] 1 S.C.R. 609, at para. 14: It has been long established, however, that an appeal by the Attorney General cannot succeed on an abstract or purely hypothetical possibility that the accused would have been convicted but for the error of law. Something more must be shown.

propositions.text: Crown need not prove verdict would necessarily differ, only that error might reasonably have materially affected acquittal.
propositions.quote: It is the duty of the Crown in order to obtain a new trial to satisfy the appellate court that the error (or errors) of the trial judge might reasonably be thought, in the concrete reality of the case at hand, to have had a material bearing on the acquittal. The Attorney General is not required, however, to persuade us that the verdict would necessarily have been different.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Crown must prove trial judge's error might have materially affected acquittal to get new trial, citing Graveline.

propositions.text: Mr. Tatton submits the trial judge based acquittal on accident defence and intoxication had no bearing on verdict
propositions.quote: Mr. Tatton submits that the trial judge based the acquittal on the defence of accident and that intoxication had no bearing on the analysis.

propositions.text: Mr. Tatton argues trial judge's error could not reasonably have affected verdict
propositions.quote: He therefore argues that the trial judge’s error cannot reasonably be thought to have affected the verdict.

propositions.text: Crown argues trial judge considered Mr. Tatton’s intoxication in verdict
propositions.quote: The Crown, on the other hand, argues that the trial judge’s reasons make it clear that he considered Mr. Tatton’s intoxication in arriving at the verdict.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues trial judge based acquittal on accident defence and error did not affect verdict; respondent argues intoxication was considered in verdict.

propositions.text: Accepts Crown's submission that intoxication played material role in outcome
propositions.quote: I accept the Crown’s submission. In my view, when the trial judge’s reasons are read in their entirety, it is apparent that Mr. Tatton’s intoxication played a material role in the outcome.

paragraphs.summary: Court accepts Crown's submission that intoxication materially influenced trial judge's verdict.

propositions.text: Trial judge focused on cause of fire and whether intoxication could be considered
propositions.quote: In his reasons, the trial judge concentrated on the cause of the fire. In particular, the question he posed was whether he could be satisfied that Mr. Tatton intentionally or recklessly started the fire in the frying pan.

propositions.text: Trial judge stated he must determine if intoxication could be considered
propositions.quote: At the outset of his analysis, the trial judge stated that to resolve this issue, he must determine whether Mr. Tatton’s intoxication could be considered.

propositions.text: Trial judge's reasons focus almost exclusively on intoxication issue
propositions.quote: The trial judge’s reasons focus almost exclusively on this issue.

propositions.text: If fire was accidental separate from alcohol role, intoxication analysis was unnecessary
propositions.quote: If, as Mr. Tatton argues, the trial judge concluded that the fire was accidental — separate and apart from any role alcohol may have played — all of this analysis was unnecessary.

propositions.text: It defies logic to suggest acquittal was not influenced by erroneous belief about intoxication
propositions.quote: In my view, it defies logic and common sense to suggest that the trial judge’s decision to acquit was not influenced by his erroneous belief that he could take into account Mr. Tatton’s state of intoxication.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds trial judge focused on intoxication in deciding cause of fire and acquittal was influenced by erroneous belief about intoxication.

propositions.text: Trial judge's concluding remarks show intoxication was central to reasonable doubt
propositions.quote: The trial judge’s concluding remarks bear this out. In finding that he was left in a state of reasonable doubt, the trial judge stated that one of the questions troubling him was whether Mr. Tatton was “mentally able to carry out such a plan, in view of his drunken condition”

propositions.text: Trial judge did not explicitly find accident but was not satisfied beyond reasonable doubt of intent
propositions.quote: Although the trial judge noted Mr. Tatton’s position that the fire was accidental, he did not explicitly make a finding of accident. Rather, he stated that he was not satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that Mr. Tatton had acted intentionally or recklessly.

propositions.text: Clear implication is intoxication caused reasonable doubt about intent
propositions.quote: the clear implication from his reasons is that it was Mr. Tatton’s state of intoxication that left him in a state of reasonable doubt as to whether Mr. Tatton acted with the requisite intent.

propositions.text: Satisfied that test in Graveline has been met
propositions.quote: That being so, I am satisfied that the test in Graveline has been met.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds trial judge's doubt about intent was due to intoxication and test in Graveline is met.

propositions.text: Allows appeal, sets aside acquittal, orders new trial
propositions.quote: For these reasons, I would allow the appeal, set aside the acquittal, and order a new trial. Appeal allowed.

propositions.text: Solicitors for appellant and respondent and intervener named
propositions.quote: Solicitor for the appellant: Attorney General of Ontario, Toronto. Solicitors for the respondent: Gorrell, Greinkie & Rémillard, Morrisburg. Solicitors for the intervener: Kapoor Barristers, Toronto.

paragraphs.summary: Court allows appeal, sets aside acquittal, orders new trial; solicitor details provided.
